clue.text: So little point in this intelligence message!

parts.note: micro means very small, so tiny

explanation.surface: A weary analyst sighs that this intelligence report has no point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So little point' reads as a complaint about the message's value; it is the wordplay, a tiny point, which is literally what the message is.
explanation.definitionFit: Spies hid documents as photographs reduced to the size of a printed full stop, easily concealed on a letter.

clue.text: Times do change for a fashionable dressmaker

indicators.note: changing the words alters them, so their letters come out in a different order

explanation.surface: Changing times mean changing styles for a fashionable dressmaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times do change' reads as a proverb; the first two words are the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Modiste is the French-derived term for a dressmaker or milliner who makes stylish clothes and hats.

clue.text: Write music about it that is synthesized

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word wraps around the second

parts.note: to write music is to compose

explanation.surface: Someone writes music about electronic sounds made on a synthesizer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Synthesized' suggests electronic music, which fits the surface; here it means put together from parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A composite thing is made up of several parts combined, just as a synthesis builds a whole from elements.

clue.text: Where French score almost is surpassed

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A match report: where the French nearly scored, they were beaten.
explanation.definitionFit: To outgo someone is to go further than them, so the past tense means exceeded or overtook.

clue.text: Playing forward, to leg?

parts.note: on as in go on, moving forward
a leg of a journey is a stage

explanation.surface: A cricket instruction: play forward, to the leg side.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture of a batsman playing forward to leg is a decoy; leg means a section of a journey. In cricket the leg side is also called the on side.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor who is playing is performing in front of an audience in the theatre.

clue.text: Floppy disk work in dusty environment?

indicators.note: being in somewhere means sitting inside it, so these pieces go within the dusty word
an environment surrounds whatever lives in it, so the dusty word wraps around what comes before

parts.note: a disk is round, the shape of the letter O
OP, short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A computer floppy disk is put to work somewhere dusty, a hazard for such media.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floppy disk' reads as one computing term, but only 'Floppy' is the definition; the disk is a round letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something drooping hangs limply, the same loose, sagging quality as being floppy.

clue.text: Shredded paper said to vanish without trace

indicators.note: shredding tears something into pieces that land jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Documents are put through the shredder so they vanish without trace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said' looks like a sound-alike signal but is simply part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To go out of sight completely and leave no sign is to become lost from view.

clue.text: More frequently, emollient is not opened

indicators.note: a thing not opened is missing its opening, so the first letter goes

explanation.surface: A tube of skin cream is more often left unopened than used.
explanation.definitionFit: Often means frequently, so the comparative form means at more frequent intervals.

clue.text: Girl friend initially providing Asian tree

indicators.note: initially says that the second word named goes at the start, before the first

explanation.surface: A girlfriend's first gift is a tree from Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' usually takes first letters; here it only puts the friend at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The palmyra is a tall fan palm of India and Sri Lanka, tapped for toddy and sugar.

clue.text: Assisted me to distribute coffee cups

indicators.note: distributing spreads things out in a new arrangement, so the preceding letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Someone helped a host hand round the coffee cups.
explanation.definitionFit: A demitasse is a small cup for after-dinner black coffee, from French for half-cup.

clue.text: He split an apple and peach

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the legendary Swiss archer who shot an apple off his son's head
second meaning: as a verb, to inform on someone

explanation.surface: Someone cuts up an apple and a peach for a fruit salad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peach' looks like another fruit beside the apple, but it is the old verb meaning to grass on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: William Tell, the Swiss hero, split an apple with an arrow; to peach is old slang for informing.

clue.text: Board game to push change no longer

parts.note: a coin of loose change withdrawn from British currency in 1984

explanation.surface: A board game is being pushed to change something that no longer works.
explanation.walkthrough: The halfpenny was a small British coin, abolished in 1984, so 'no longer' marks it as obsolete change.
explanation.definitionFit: Shove-halfpenny is a British pub game, sliding coins up a marked board with the palm.

clue.text: Letter reproduced in elite, with PS

indicators.note: reproducing makes a new copy, here one whose letters come out in another order

explanation.surface: A letter is typed in Elite typeface, with a postscript added.
explanation.walkthrough: Elite is a typewriter typeface, so the surface is about a typed letter; 'with' joins the two parts of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An epistle is a formal or literary letter, like those of the apostles in the New Testament.

clue.text: Clear date fixed for rent

indicators.note: something fixed has been altered or rigged, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A landlord sets a clear date by which the rent must be paid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like the payment to a landlord; it is the past participle of rend, meaning torn.
explanation.definitionFit: Rent, the past form of rend, means torn apart, and lacerated flesh is jaggedly torn.

clue.text: Pick up and report rumour

parts.note: to pick up a sound is to hear it

explanation.surface: An instruction to catch a rumour and pass it on.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearsay is information received from others rather than witnessed, which is what gossip and rumour are.

clue.text: Victoria, possibly — queen from whom our rulers come?

parts.note: Victoria is a London railway terminus

explanation.surface: Queen Victoria is named as the ancestor of Britain's royal rulers.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal surface casts Victoria as the monarch and rulers as kings; Victoria is a London station, and rulers are measuring sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: A stationer's shop sells office and writing supplies, including the straight-edged rulers used for drawing lines.

clue.text: Introduction of umpire in March

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it is placed inside the second word

parts.note: REF, short for referee, a match official like an umpire

explanation.surface: An umpire is introduced to the game in the month of March.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital M makes 'March' look like the month; it is the verb, and the umpire goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A preface is the opening section of a book, an introduction written before the main text.

clue.text: Ballet's originator switching Wooster's parts

indicators.note: switching the two halves moves the back half round to the front

parts.note: Bertie Wooster, P. G. Wodehouse's comic hero, is Bertram in full, read as two parts

explanation.surface: Someone who started a ballet swaps roles with Wodehouse's Wooster.
explanation.walkthrough: Bertie Wooster is the foolish young gentleman of Wodehouse's Jeeves stories; 'parts' means sections of his name, not roles.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Marie Rambert founded Ballet Rambert, Britain's oldest dance company, in 1926.

clue.text: Maximum holding one can manage single-handed

definitions.text: Maximum holding one can manage single-handed

parts.words: Maximum holding one can manage single-handed
parts.note: surface reading: the largest business or estate one person could run alone
setter's reading: literally with one hand, so the amount one hand can grasp

explanation.surface: A smallholder wonders how much land one person can farm without help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding' suggests property and 'single-handed' means alone; read literally, they mean what one hand can grip.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is the quantity a closed hand can grasp at once, so it is the most one hand holds.

clue.text: Old hat of chief, and superb cape

parts.note: arch as an adjective means chief, as in arch-enemy
A1 means first-rate; the 1 is read as the letter I
C is the map abbreviation for cape

explanation.surface: An old hat belonging to a chief, worn with a superb cape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old hat' looks like a garment beside the cape, but it is the idiom for outdated. A1 counts as AI in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Something old hat is stale and out of date, as anything archaic belongs to a long-gone era.

clue.text: Deficiency that causes increased cardiac weakness

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a lack of something
second meaning: the proverb says it makes the heart grow fonder

explanation.surface: A medical note on a deficiency that weakens the heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds clinical, but 'cardiac weakness' is a fondness of the heart, as in the proverb about being apart from a loved one.
explanation.definitionFit: A lack or want of something is an absence, and the proverb says being apart makes the heart grow fonder.

clue.text: Bloke allowed to supply wreath

parts.note: a chap is a bloke, a man

explanation.surface: A man is permitted to provide a funeral wreath.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplet is a garland or circlet of flowers worn on the head.

clue.text: Key of C learnt haphazardly

indicators.note: done haphazardly means without order, so the letters come out jumbled

explanation.surface: A music pupil has picked up the key of C in a slapdash way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key of C' is a musical phrase, but 'Key' alone is the definition, an adjective meaning crucial.
explanation.definitionFit: A key issue is crucial or most important, just as a central one is principal and essential.

clue.text: This, from Latin, is smart? No, badly done

definitions.text: This, from Latin, is smart? No, badly done

indicators.note: something badly done is botched and comes out wrong, so the preceding letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A schoolchild's clever rendering of Latin is scorned as anything but smart.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: the letters of 'Latin is smart no' rearrange to the answer, and a botched rendering from Latin is exactly what it describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A rendering from another language done badly, so the meaning is lost or garbled, is a faulty translation.

clue.text: Money taken from chapel funds

indicators.note: taking something from a phrase means lifting a run of consecutive letters out of it

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: Someone has been pilfering from the chapel collection.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelf is an old, disparaging word for wealth or riches, especially ill-gotten gains.

clue.text: Like a neat high jump in the nursery

definitions.text: Like a neat high jump in the nursery

parts.note: surface reading: a tidy athletic leap, as at a sports day
setter's reading: neat is an old word for cattle, so the jumper is a cow
the nursery rhyme Hey Diddle Diddle, in which the cow jumped over the moon

explanation.surface: A child makes a tidy high jump in the playroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' reads as tidy; it is the archaic word for a cow. The nursery rhyme cow jumped over the moon, so its leap went beyond it.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes something passing beyond the moon, as the cow's leap in the rhyme did.

clue.text: Not easy to move team-leader into firm

indicators.note: going into something means being placed inside the other word
the leader of a word is its opening letter, the one at the front

explanation.surface: A team captain who is hard to shift is moving into a business firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Team-leader' looks like a captain; it is the first letter of 'team'. 'Firm' is a business on the surface but means solid here.
explanation.definitionFit: A stolid person is impassive and unemotional, hard to stir or rouse to feeling.

clue.text: Using signs to show largest development round university

indicators.note: a development changes the shape of something, so the letters are rearranged
going round something means surrounding it, so the scrambled word wraps the abbreviation

parts.note: the letters of largest rearranged, then split around the next piece
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Signs are put up to show the biggest development around a university campus.
explanation.definitionFit: Gestural communication relies on movements of the hands and body rather than spoken words.
